title: Tests that catch bugs
description:
This time **you write the tests**, and the checker judges how good they are.

Somebody has written a function that should behave like this:

> `clampTo(value, low, high)` returns `value` if it lies between `low` and `high` inclusive, `low` if it is smaller, and `high` if it is larger.

Write `bool passesMyTests(ClampFn clampTo)`. It receives an implementation, tries it on inputs of your choosing, and returns `true` only if every answer is right.

The checker hands your function one correct implementation, which must pass, and several subtly broken ones, each of which must **fail**. This is called *mutation testing*: tests are only worth something if they notice when the code is wrong.

Think about where implementations go wrong: at the edges, exactly on a boundary, with negative numbers, and when `low` equals `high`.

solution.solution.cpp:
using ClampFn = int (*)(int value, int low, int high);

bool passesMyTests(ClampFn clampTo)
{
    return clampTo(5, 0, 10) == 5      // inside
        && clampTo(-3, 0, 10) == 0     // below
        && clampTo(42, 0, 10) == 10    // above
        && clampTo(0, 0, 10) == 0      // exactly on the low edge
        && clampTo(10, 0, 10) == 10    // exactly on the high edge
        && clampTo(1, 0, 10) == 1      // just inside each edge
        && clampTo(9, 0, 10) == 9
        && clampTo(-7, -5, -1) == -5   // a negative range
        && clampTo(-3, -5, -1) == -3
        && clampTo(3, -5, -1) == -1
        && clampTo(4, 7, 7) == 7       // a range of one value
        && clampTo(7, 7, 7) == 7
        && clampTo(9, 7, 7) == 7;
}

hints: For every boundary, test the value exactly on it and the values on either side. Then repeat with a range that does not start at zero, and one that is entirely negative.
lessonTitle: Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling
